The project, built around the rev A PCB frame

Fly-Brain drone: the complete build

A small ESP32-S3 camera quadcopter steered by a simulated fruit fly brain on a laptop. The frame is a custom PCB that also carries the motor drivers, so the build is: order the board, print a few small parts, solder, and fly. Press Build guide to assemble it in 3D.

Frame 2-layer PCB, 83 × 83 mm Motor to motor 95 mm Weight ~68–76 g Parts $43.31 + PCB ~$2–5 Status rev A, not built yet

    Build guide

    Do the steps in order; each only needs what came before it. Tap a step to see it in 3D. The order follows pcb/README.md, with the fixes from the review below.

    We only bought red wire. Mark the ground end of each wire with a black marker or a strip of tape; the colors here only tell the wires apart.

      PCB review, rev A

      I reran pcb/gen.py: every spacing, edge, drill and connectivity check passes, and the netlist matches the design. The board is sound. Two things need attention before you solder, and a few are worth knowing.

      Fix before soldering

      Cut the MOSFET tabs off

      The outlines are drawn for the plastic body only, 9.2 mm long. With its metal tab an IRLB8721 is about 15.5 mm, so lying in its outline the tab reaches the motor's + and − pads and the end of the diode. The + pad is battery plus and the tab is the drain, so the motor would run flat out as soon as the battery goes in, and the motor pads would be buried. Cut each tab flush with the body. The README's assembly step and a "CUT TAB" note on the silkscreen should say so.

      Fix before flying

      Keep the battery off the pin ends

      The MPU6050 header and the rear row of jumper pads sit right above the battery, and clipped leads are sharp enough to puncture a LiPo pouch. Clip them flush, cover them with a strip of tape, and use the printed tray, which holds the battery 2 mm below the board.

      Handled by the printed parts

      The rear spacer hole is behind the ESP32

      The rear screw hole is at y = −34.5 mm, but the ESP32 outline ends at −30.4 mm, so a plain spacer there would touch nothing. The printed rear spacer has a shelf that reaches 4 mm under the board's rear edge.

      Handled by the printed parts

      Motor collars sit on top of the board

      An 8.5 mm motor in an 8.8 mm hole leaves 0.15 mm for a collar inside the hole, too thin to print. The printed collar sits on top around the hole and is glued down. To press-fit the motors instead, set MOTOR_HOLE_D to 8.6 in gen.py.

      Set during assembly

      The props pass over the ESP32

      The prop discs overlap the ESP32's corners, and on 8 mm spacers its top is about 13.7 mm above the board. Set each motor's top 16 mm above the board, 6 mm above its collar, so the props clear it.

      Good to know

      Battery current runs through thermal spokes

      BAT−, BAT+ and each MOSFET source join their pour through four 0.45 mm spokes. That's fine for a few amps; solder those joints generously. Wider spokes on BAT+ and BAT− would be cheap insurance in a rev B.

      Good to know

      Tight resistor spacing and the SD slot

      The resistors use 7.62 mm pad spacing, tight for a ¼ W part, so bend the leads right at the body. On some ESP32-S3 camera boards GPIO 38 and 40 also go to the SD card slot: leave it empty, or move those two signals to GPIO 1 and 2.

      Good to know

      The 40 g target in frame/README.md

      The motors, battery and ESP32 alone come to about 38 g, so a 40 g drone isn't reachable with these parts. Expect about 68–76 g; the thrust check below covers it.

      Checked and fine

      • The Gerbers in pcb/out match a fresh run of gen.py (only line endings differ), and the KiCad file is still the generated one, so gen.py is still the master copy.
      • Every net matches the design: battery plus, ground, 3.3 V, SCL, SDA, INT, four gate nets and four drain nets.
      • MOSFET pin order: lying metal side down with the legs toward the center, the gate is on the left seen from the center, and all four footprints follow that.
      • Diode stripes and C1's plus are on battery plus; the GY-521 pin order is VCC, GND, SCL, SDA, XDA, XCL, AD0, INT with VCC on the square pad.
      • The 10 kΩ pull-downs keep the motors off while the ESP32 boots, and the chosen pins avoid the camera, PSRAM, USB and strapping pins.
      • Hole sizes fit the leads: 1.1 mm for the MOSFETs, 1.0 mm for the diodes and motor leads, 1.2 mm for the battery, 0.8 mm for the jumper wires.

      Order the PCB

      Upload the Gerber zip to JLCPCB or PCBWay. Boards under 100 × 100 mm usually cost about $2–5 for five, plus shipping. Check the factory's Gerber viewer before paying: it should show the X shape, four motor holes, two screw holes and 60 plated holes.

      The same zip as pcb/out/fly-drone-gerbers.zip.

      Layers2
      Size83.2 × 83.2 mm (detected from the outline)
      Thickness1.0 mm, or 1.2 mm if you want it stiffer
      Surface finishHASL lead-free
      Copper1 oz
      Quantity5, the minimum and about the same price
      Remove order numberYes, if it's free

      Print the parts

      Everything prints in one job on the H2D with no supports, about 7 g of PLA on the drone. These parts replace the printed frame from before: the PCB is the frame now.

      The zip has the full build plate plus each part on its own.
      PartQtyOn the bedWhat it does
      Motor collar4Flange down8.5 mm inside; glued on top around each motor hole
      Foot4Flange downOptional; glued under each motor hole, lead slot toward the center
      Battery tray1Rails downIts two towers take the M2 × 16 screws and hold the battery 2 mm off the board
      ESP32 spacer, front1Standing8 mm, blind hole for the screw
      ESP32 spacer, rear1Shelf down8 mm; the shelf reaches under the ESP32
      Camera stand1Base downGlued on the front tongue; tilts the camera up 10°
      Motor fit test1FlatPrint it first: rings of 8.3, 8.5 and 8.7 mm, from the tab end

      PLA, 0.2 mm layers, 3 walls, 15% infill, supports off. If the 8.5 mm fit-test ring isn't the snug one, the collars need the size that is.

      Connections

      The PCB does almost all the wiring. The ESP32's pinout couldn't be confirmed from its listing, so the board brings every signal to labeled jumper pads, and short wires go from each pad up into the ESP32's pin holes from below. Check the pins against your board's silkscreen before soldering.

      PadESP32 pinWhat it is
      G1GPIO 21Motor 1 gate
      G2GPIO 47Motor 2 gate
      G3GPIO 14Motor 3 gate
      G4GPIO 38Motor 4 gate
      SCLGPIO 42MPU6050 clock
      SDAGPIO 41MPU6050 data
      INTGPIO 40MPU6050 interrupt
      3V3 (front)3V33.3 V supply in
      GND (front)GNDGround
      Rear padBuck-boost
      VINVIN
      GNDGND
      3V3VOUT
      Bridge EN to VIN on the module

      Wires to cut

      Lengths are measured along each wire's path in the model, plus 10 mm to strip and solder. Cut them a little long and trim. The motor leads and the camera ribbon come attached.

      #WireFromToLength

      The ESP32 pin positions in the model follow the typical layout of these boards (J1 with 3V3 at the top, J3 with GND at the top), so the jumper lengths are estimates until the real board arrives.

      Software

      The brain runs on a laptop; the drone keeps itself stable and does what the brain says. The drone camera streams video over WiFi, the laptop pulls out visual features with OpenCV (looming, sideways motion, small targets), stimulates the matching neurons (LPLC2 and LC4, HS cells, LC10), reads the descending neurons (DNa01 and DNa02 for steering, the Giant Fiber for escape), and sends yaw, climb and forward commands back over UDP. The target is 5–10 brain decisions per second.

      Drone firmware (drone/)

      ESP-Drone (Crazyflie-based) in VS Code with PlatformIO, remapped to the pins above. PSRAM has to be enabled:

      [env:esp32s3cam]
platform = espressif32
board = esp32-s3-devkitc-1
framework = arduino
board_build.arduino.memory_type = qio_opi
board_build.flash_size = 16MB
build_flags = -DBOARD_HAS_PSRAM
monitor_speed = 115200
      1. MPU6050 roll and pitch over serial.
      2. One motor at a time with a slow PWM ramp, props off, a spare 716 motor first.
      3. Camera MJPEG stream over WiFi, 160 × 120 or QVGA, the ESP32 as the access point.
      4. UDP commands (throttle, roll, pitch, yaw) from the laptop.

      Brain (brain/)

      Shiu et al.'s whole-brain model (philshiu/Drosophila_brain_model): Brian2 with the FlyWire v783 connectome, about 139,000 neurons. It's far too big for the ESP32, which is why it lives on the laptop.

      1. Phase 1: get the model running; activating the sugar-sensing neurons should make MN9 fire.
      2. Phase 2: webcam eyes: an OpenCV looming detector stimulates LPLC2 and LC4, and you read the Giant Fiber. Neuron IDs come from FlyWire Codex.
      3. Later: swap the features for a full fly-eye model (flyvis, flygym).

      Will it lift?

      Each motor has to push about half the drone's weight for a 2:1 thrust margin, which it needs to climb and steer. Once it's built, set the weight to what the kitchen scale says.

      Needed per motor
      One prop can make, at about 75% of the listed RPM

      Thrust is estimated as C_T × air density × (rev/s)² × diameter⁴. The real check: once the motors arrive, hold one motor and prop down on a kitchen scale and read the grams it pushes.

      Before the first flight

      Work down the list with the props off until the last two. Unplug the battery whenever USB is connected. Charge the LiPo at 500 mA or less, off the drone, and never unattended.
